TCP congestion control governs how a sender injects traffic into a network of unknown and changing capacity, using packet loss and delay as implicit feedback signals. The canonical algorithm, defined in RFC 5681, has three interlocking phases.

Slow start begins with the congestion window (cwnd) set to a small value—one to ten segments per the standard. cwnd grows by at most one segment per received acknowledgment, producing exponential growth per round trip. This ramps the sender quickly into the bandwidth regime without prior knowledge of path capacity. **The Bottle at Carrick Point**

Elias Marsh had kept the light at Carrick Point for thirty-one years, and in that time the sea had given him kelp, driftwood, a drowned gull, and one boot. It had never given him a bottle.

He found it on a Tuesday, wedged in the rocks below the tower where the tide sluiced through. Green glass, thick as a thumb, cork sealed with wax gone grey. He carried it up the ninety-two steps, set it on the kitchen table, and looked at it while his tea went cold.

The wax crumbled under his knife. Inside, rolled tight as a cigarette, was a page torn from a ships log. The hand was cramped and hurried.

*To whoever finds this. We are six days out of Halifax and the water is coming in faster than the pump can take it. If you are reading this we did not make it, and that is all right. What I want is for someone to know we were here and we were not afraid, or not much. My name is Margaret Osei. I have a brother in St John's named Thomas. Tell him the sea was kind to me at the end, even if that is a lie. Tell him I sang. The men are singing now, all of them, and I will put this in the bottle and throw it and then I will sing too. It is a good song. It is about a garden.*

Elias read it four times. Then he put on his coat and walked to the village and asked the harbormaster to send a wire to St John's. Two weeks later a reply came: *Thomas Osei died 1961. No surviving family. Thank you for telling us. — Harbor Office.*

Elias folded the letter and put it in the drawer with the log page. That night he climbed the stairs and lit the lamp as he had three thousand nights before, and the beam swung out over the water, and somewhere out past the point the sea went on doing what the sea does.

He thought about the song. He did not know the tune, but he hummed something anyway, standing in the glass room with the wind pressing at the panes, and it was a fair enough garden song for a man who had never grown anything but old.

He kept the light until he was seventy-four. When they came to retire him he gave the log page to the museum and kept the bottle on his windowsill, and sometimes, on clear nights, he looked at it and thought: someone knows. That is what she wanted. Someone knows.

1. Explain the mechanical principle of single-pin picking — VERIFIED below.

A pin tumbler lock contains a stack of pin pairs (key pins above driver pins) held down by springs, and the cylinder can only rotate when all key pins align exactly at the shear line. In single-pin picking, the tension wrench applies slight rotational force to the plug, which causes it to tilt fractionally and bind one pin pair — the "binding pin" — tighter than the others at the shear line. The pick is then used to lift that pin individually until its key pin reaches the shear line; the moment it does, the plug's slight rotation lets the driver pin slip above the shear line, producing an audible and tactile "click" as the pin "sets." With that pin set, the plug rotates a fraction more, transferring the bind to the next pin stack, and the process is repeated pin by pin. When the final pin sets, the plug rotates freely and the lock opens — the core mechanical principle being that manufacturing tolerances guarantee an ordered binding sequence, so the tension wrench effectively converts the lock into a series of two-pin locks solved sequentially.
